questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: partly to be able to participate in an international setting, and partly to end up in a generally cool place

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. The school provided plenty of information upon arrival

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had a couple of orientation days where the school's exchange office told us about all the practical matters we needed to be aware of while we were in the country

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy to find a place to live. At first, I got help from the school itself, which had a list of landlords they could vouch for. However, many of the rental periods were for a full year, so it wasn’t worth it when I was only going to be there for half a year. So I ended up finding a landlord on the “Zillow” platform, which works a bit like Airbnb, but for longer stays. It worked out great, and my landlord, Ara, was simply the sweetest person.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it's very common to live off campus, and that you can also save quite a bit of money on rent by living off campus

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was fairly reliable and, from a technical standpoint, worked much the same way as it did in Copenhagen. However, enrollment in the school’s courses was on a first-come, first-served basis, which meant that you had to act quickly and know in advance which courses you intended to sign up for.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The school offered a lot of support—everything from psychological counseling to academic guidance. I especially relied on the help from the course registration office, which was a huge help when I had to register for classes for my second quarter there.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to sign up for all the classes I wanted, so I'd say it was pretty successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be sure to check in advance which courses sound interesting so you’ll be ready when course registration opens. Of course, remember to choose your courses based on your pre-approval so you don’t waste your time during the exchange program.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some of the courses were, in a sense, very much on par with what one would expect from courses here at home. However, there were also some courses that were a bit below par. In my second quarter, though, I took a graduate-level course, which fortunately raised the overall level considerably.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style was much more similar to what you see in high schools here at home, which I actually really liked. In Copenhagen, there’s a very clear hierarchy between teachers and students, whereas teachers in the U.S. got much more involved in the students’ work and encouraged them to participate in class, including by speaking up during class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
In my first quarter, I took the following courses:
ECN 111A Economic History
ECN 122 Game Theory 
ECN 134 Financial Economics
ECN 164 International Finance

On my second quarter, I took the following courses:
ECN 160B International Macroeconomics
ECN 260D Topics in International Macroeconomics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I highly recommend ECN 164. It’s a really exciting course that provides economics students with a great introduction to the world of finance. The course is structured exceptionally well, allowing you to both solve real-world case studies and work on an individual project exploring investment opportunities in a country of your choice anywhere in the world. In addition, you’re kept on your toes with quizzes every Friday in the course.
Dr. Ina Simonovska, who teaches the course, is also an exceptionally skilled instructor with extensive real-world experience. She also teaches ECN 260D, which is highly recommended if you’re interested in macroeconomics at a more challenging level.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The school has certain health requirements that you must meet before arriving. That meant I had to get two chickenpox vaccinations before I left. It was a somewhat unexpected expense.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: With all the talk about inflation in the U.S., I was a little worried that food and drinks would be expensive during my stay, but when I arrived, it turned out that food prices were actually very similar to those back home in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I decided to join the fraternity, Tau Kappa Epsilon. It was definitely one of the best decisions I made socially. I made a lot of American friends through it. Among other things, I celebrated Christmas at one of the guys’ places and New Year’s at another one of their places. I’m still in touch with many of them, which is great.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The school offered all kinds of different organizations and clubs. There were clubs for just about every major sport, and there were organizations for every political or religious belief. In addition, there was, of course, a wide variety of fraternities and sororities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I especially recommend joining a fraternity. It’s an easy way to make lots of American friends and meet people who aren’t just studying the same major as you. It’s also a great alternative to various sports clubs if you’d rather not join one. Fraternities also open the door to a large network of alumni, which can be very rewarding.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Start with the “low-hanging fruit.” In other words, try some of the many fun restaurants and eateries that we don’t have back home in Denmark. Take a weekend trip to San Francisco or go hiking in Lake Tahoe or Yosemite. It’s really worth the drive. I also ended up organizing a trip to Hawaii with some of the other Europeans, which I wouldn’t have wanted to miss for the world. The rail network is relatively extensive in California, so you can also easily get to Los Angeles or San Diego. Flixbus is also a good and inexpensive alternative to the trains.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: At first, you had to get past the language barrier with your “Danglish,” but fortunately, Americans are so open and welcoming that it's very easy to adapt to their culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just be yourself and be open. Many Americans aren’t shy about asking you questions before or after a lecture. We Danes may have a slight tendency to spread out in a lecture hall and, in any case, avoid sitting next to anyone we don’t know. The opposite is somewhat true for Americans. Many of them are also wide-eyed when you tell them you’ve come all the way from Copenhagen. To them, Copenhagen has a bit of a “paradise” status, and while many of them have never been there, they all say they’d love to visit Copenhagen someday. That’s a great topic for a friendly chat before a lecture.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I actually think Americans are quite similar to us Danes, so I can't really think of any major differences that made my stay difficult.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Definitely the openness and friendliness of Americans. I sometimes miss that here in Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Be patient at first. You’ll definitely make a lot of new friends during your stay.
2) Be curious about the big experiences, but especially the little ones.
3) Go to a party at Tau Kappa Epsilon. They definitely throw the coolest frat parties on campus.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: not exactly

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: all the friends I made from all over the world

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: to step outside their Copenhagen bubble and try to match the Americans' openness.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
